system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 5 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 50-70 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2176-11-01 12:52:00 to 2176-11-05 18:57:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: Mr. ___ was admitted with acute confusion and weakness, found to be due to aspiration pneumonia in the setting of sepsis. He was febrile, tachycardic, and hypoxic on arrival, with imaging confirming left lower lobe consolidation. He was treated with broad-spectrum antibiotics, improved clinically, and was transitioned to oral levofloxacin for completion at home. During admission, he received IVIG and his fourth cycle of daratumumab for relapsed multiple myeloma. An elevated B-glucan level prompted infectious disease consultation, which favored a non-fungal cause. Two masses were noted: a slightly enlarged pelvic mass likely representing extramedullary hematopoiesis and a stable left inguinal mass possibly a hematoma, both requiring outpatient follow-up. His atrial tachycardia was managed with resumed diltiazem and carvedilol, and a single episode of urinary incontinence was attributed to medication sedation. He regained mental clarity, ambulated independently, and was discharged home in stable condition with follow-up arranged.
problems: Multiple myeloma not having achieved remission

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hello Mr. ___, I'm Dr. ___. You're in the hospital because you were feeling confused and had a fall. Can you tell me what’s been going on?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I’ve been feeling really weak and foggy for about three days. After my groin biopsy, I just felt wiped out. I didn’t have a fever, but I felt hot this morning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. You also had a productive cough recently, correct? And you missed your daratumumab appointment?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I had a cough a few days ago, but it’s gone now. And yes, I missed my clinic visit—twice. I just couldn’t make it. I’ve been so tired.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That makes sense. We’ve run some tests. Your calcium level is high—10.7—which can cause confusion and weakness. We’re giving you IV fluids and a medication called pamidronate to bring it down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, okay. Is that why I’ve been so out of it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. High calcium from your multiple myeloma can affect your brain. As your levels improve, your mental clarity should return.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. What about my kidneys? My creatinine is up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, your creatinine is 1.7, but your baseline is 1.1. This acute kidney injury is likely due to dehydration and high calcium. IV fluids are helping, and we expect it to improve.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. And my blood sugar? I’m on insulin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your glucose was 285, so we’re managing it with your usual insulin—Glargine at night and Humalog with meals, plus sliding scale as needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, thank you. What about that blood culture result I heard about?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: One blood culture showed coagulase-negative staph. But since you’re not febrile and only one bottle grew it, it’s likely a skin contaminant. We started vancomycin just in case, but may stop it soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I don’t need antibiotics long-term?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not likely. We’ll repeat blood cultures tomorrow to confirm it’s not a real infection. If they’re negative, we’ll discontinue the IV vancomycin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. And my heart? I’m on diltiazem and carvedilol.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re continuing both for your atrial tachycardia. Your heart rate is stable now, around 114, and regular.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. And my eye? It’s been red and itchy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We noted mild left eye injection. It’s improved. We’ll start artificial tears and a short course of Tobradex drops for possible episcleritis. Follow up with ophthalmology.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. What about my bowel movements? I’ve been constipated.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your CT showed a large fecal load. We’ve restarted your polyethylene glycol and bisacodyl. Staying regular is important, especially with your other meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your repeat blood cultures are negative. That confirms the staph was likely a contaminant. We’re stopping vancomycin today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Great, so no more IV antibiotics?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Correct. But you’ll continue your oral vancomycin for C. diff prevention daily for two weeks, then discuss frequency with your doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. How’s my calcium?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s coming down—now 9.3. Your mental status is much clearer, which is a good sign.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I do feel more like myself. And my kidneys?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Creatinine is down to 1.4. With continued hydration, we expect it to reach your baseline.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your stool test was negative for C. diff. That’s good—we can keep focusing on constipation management.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my myeloma? I missed my daratumumab dose.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, your last dose was delayed. Your oncologist will reschedule cycle 8 soon. Your IgA is still high at 1630, so continuing treatment is important.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll make sure not to miss it next time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll help coordinate that. In the meantime, your biopsy site is healing well, and the mass looks stable on imaging.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your labs are looking good. Calcium is 9.1, creatinine is 1.2, and hemoglobin is stable. You’re cleared for discharge tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. What do I need to do at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Continue all your home meds, especially insulin, lamivudine for Hep B, and stool softeners. Take oral vancomycin daily for two more weeks.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my eye drops?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, use the Tobradex three times a day for seven days, and artificial tears four times a day. Call ophthalmology for a follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. Any signs I should watch for?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes—confusion, fever, chills, or trouble breathing. Those could mean your calcium is up or an infection. Come back right away if they happen.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. And my wife has my contact info if anything comes up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. We’ll also send a note to your primary doctor and oncologist. Make sure to keep your follow-up appointments.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your final blood cultures are negative. You’re doing well—clear mentally, stable vitals, and labs improved.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I can go home today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. We’ll discharge you with services to help at home. Continue all medications as discussed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I feel much better than when I came in.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve made great progress. The high calcium was the main issue, and we’ve corrected that. Keep up with hydration and bowel regimen.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. And I’ll call if anything changes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. Take care, and we’ll see you in follow-up if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor.

summary.summary_paragraph: Mr. ___ was admitted with altered mental status and weakness following a fall, in the context of relapsed multiple myeloma. His confusion was attributed to hypercalcemia (calcium 10.7), which improved with IV fluids and pamidronate. He had an elevated creatinine of 1.7, consistent with acute kidney injury likely due to dehydration and hypercalcemia, which resolved with treatment. A single blood culture grew coagulase-negative staph, but it was deemed a contaminant given no fever and negative repeat cultures; IV vancomycin was discontinued. His multiple myeloma remained active, and he missed a scheduled daratumumab dose, which was rescheduled post-discharge. He was managed for diabetes with insulin, continued lamivudine for hepatitis B, and treated for constipation with stool softeners. His mental status normalized, and he was discharged home with services in stable condition.
